utterances.text: Yes, I would. I believe that the Muslims were waiting for just one more thing, and that was support by the NATO airforce.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And there were MUP forces engaged in Srbinje, at the Lucevik facility, Mount Trebevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of this facility, what is the Lucevik facility?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: The Lucevik facility, sir? If you're not familiar with it, I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is something in the territory of Trnovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Right, sir. And that's what I'm really talking about is there was fierce fighting during this period of time, June, early July, in the Trnovo battlefield. Can we agree on that?

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree, but the only thing I know about that is that it was really bad. It was terrible.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And do you recall, sir, that Ljubomir Borovcanin was commanding those MUP forces on the Trnovo front? General Borovcanin here today, just so the record is clear.

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, but I believe that you're right. Mount Jahorina is on the way from Pale to Trnovo. Jahorina was on that route, so I believe you're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, I just want to ask you about one other document.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: If we could have 4D251 e-court, very quickly, please. And if we could scroll down on the B/C/S just a little bit. Perfect. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked a number of questions yesterday about the police officers' training course and the curriculum and who the instructors were. Let me just ask you first, I think you told us that policing theory would have been taught by MUP instructors, professors or professional instructors that were not members of the special police brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the instructors were professors from the school of the interior affairs, that is, lecturers; and instructors were from the police brigade, from the special police brigade. This is just an accident. Dragomir Zivkovic was a deputy and a commander of a detachment in Trebinje, and it seems that most of his policemen from his unit attended the course. That's why he was their most senior officer while they were on the training course.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Okay, sir. I didn't mean to distract you with the document just yet. I was just asking you a general question. So I am not interested in that individual that you were just asking about. But following up on what you've just told us, is it fair to say that in terms of the sort of hands-on instruction, shall we say, the diving, martial arts, marksmanship, that type of instruction would be been conducted by members of the special police brigade during the police training course that you talked about?

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, those were mostly pre-war members of special police brigades. They were masters in martial arts, and while they were in their units they were trained for very specialist tasks, such as diving, mountaineering and other such tasks. The school of internal affairs did not have such professionals on their staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Now, if we look at this document, sir, just for my last question. If you see in the second paragraph in your language where it refers to the current agreement reached with the special police brigade deputy commander. Do you see that paragraph, sir? And it refers to three names.

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: You were asked by my friend yesterday about the first and third names, and I think you identified them as not being members of the special police brigade. I want to ask you about the person in the middle that's listed here, Ljuban Poprzen. Who was he, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: A colleague of mine, a pre-war special. Before the war, he was a member of a special police unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And he, in fact, became an instructor at Jahorina, did he not, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He became an instructor even before Jahorina was established. From 1982 to 1992, he underwent continuous training courses in the special unit of the former republican Ministry of the Interior in Sarajevo. He was a man who had undergone a 10-year-long training stint that enabled him to perform these tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: And in 1995, he was a special police brigade instructor, correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: MILAN STOJCINOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And a very serious one.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Sir, I thank you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there redirect, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, maybe it will be convenient to take a break now, and I will discuss whether I have some questions for re-examination of the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We will have a 25-minute break now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. [French on English channel] One moment because we have...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Apologies, mistake by the interpreters. Wrong microphone. Apologies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's okay. Now you can proceed, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just wanted to alert you all to a potential --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is the witness going to return to the courtroom or not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour. I don't think there is any need from our side because there will be no redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I am talking -- I'm referring to the curtains, actually. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is just a potential scheduling -- well, problem. As you know, Mr. Dunjic, the expert, it looks like he will be testifying tomorrow if -- we think. And you may recall that Chris Mitchell handled him the last time he was here, and Chris has just earlier in the day gone home with what looks like a pretty bad flu, and he was the one lawyer that was prepared and learned the report, had the documents ready in what was a technical situation. So we're not sure he's going to be back tomorrow to be -- and it doesn't really look like it, frankly. We wanted him to get better. So it's likely that any cross-examination would have gone over the long holiday, but it would be regrettable if that had to happen. But I just wanted to alert you to that. Mr. Nicholls is now on the Karadzic team. He is -- unless we bring him in for a special appearance, he's just -- to let you know, he is on another team, now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's start from here. You don't need this witness any further, Mr. Lazarevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. We don't need him either, no? So we release the witness. Madam Usher can thank him on our behalf and wish him a safe journey. The matter raised by Mr. McCloskey. So Dunjic is not the first witness we have in line. We have another one preceding him, Mr. Markovic. How long do you expect your examination-in-chief of Mr. Markovic to last? I know that you have given a forecast, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Our estimate of 45 minutes stands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 45 minutes. And I don't estimate there will be any particular cross-examination from the other Defence teams. From the Prosecution side? Yes, Mr. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Vanderpuye says probably at the most an hour and a half and, you know, given -- it may not even be that much. But it's hard to say until we hear the direct, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: We estimated on behalf of Drago Nikolic 30 minutes, and I will use the 30 minutes, Mr. President, and actually, I wanted to advise the Trial Chamber that maybe I will go a bit over those 30 minutes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So that's -- thank you so much, Mr. Bourgon. So that's 45 plus 30, an hour and 15 minutes, and an hour and 15 minutes, roughly another hour, hour and a half, Prosecution. That will take about three hours maximum, as I imagine, because I haven't heard anyone else showing an interest in cross-examining the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There are no other witnesses available for...

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. And Mr. Zivanovic, you haven't air-lifted an investigator?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This morning, I contacted witness and victims unit, and they need the five working days to provide his visas. So he cannot come to The Hague before Friday, next Friday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. This cross-examination of Dunjic, what were your anticipations time-wise?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: An hour and a half is our estimate, and you know, there's documents and other material that I have seen, that Mr. Mitchell was showing me. And I also forgot to mention, I can't be here until about, well, 1.30 tomorrow because I'm at my son's graduation, so I can't be here in the morning either. So I would say about an hour, hour and a half is our estimate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And how much time do you require for leading?

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: We have 45 minutes estimated, but I must say --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With Dunjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: -- with Professor Dunjic, but we may go slightly over, not greatly over but slightly over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So putting it all together, it seems that there is no chance that we come to the cross-examination of Dunjic tomorrow in any case. It also seems that at most we may have half an hour of testimony -- half an hour of testimony. Yes, Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. President, for interrupting. We don't, of course, oppose the request by the Prosecution for an adjournment until Tuesday or until such time as Mr. Mitchell is available. It would be our fervent request and hope that we could present our examination-in-chief immediately prior to the beginning of the cross-examination. And as I say, it's not a particularly long examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We've given advance notice of the problem. I think much depends on how long we are going to take -- how much time we are going to take with the next witness, first. I think we'll give you a decision tomorrow because if we are left with 15, 20 minutes, it's one thing. If we are left with an hour or so, it's another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll give Mr. Mitchell a chance to recover. So we'll finish with this witness first, and then unless things have changed and Mr. Mitchell is available tomorrow, we will adjourn after that. But if he is fit to come and resume his work, then, of course, we will continue and we will proceed with Dunjic tomorrow. Otherwise, we adjourn until Tuesday because Monday, as you will recall, we have to give the courtroom to the Krajisnik Appeals Chamber. All right. Documents, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this point I would kindly ask to deal with documents once this next witness finishes because I use a couple of documents which I only had hard copies. We don't have numbers for these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- if it's convenient. I already spoke to my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And Mr. Josse didn't make any use of any documents. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: We had no documents, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had no documents either. All right. So that matter is deferred until later. The next witness, please. Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Markovic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You have been summoned as an expert witness by the Borovcanin Defence team. Before you start giving evidence, our rules require that you make a solemn declaration to the effect that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth. Madam Usher is going to give you the text of this declaration. Please read it out aloud, and that will be your solemn commitment with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Please make yourself comfortable. Mr. Gosnell will be putting some questions to you in relation to the report that you prepared, and then he will be followed by others on cross-examination. Mr. Gosnell.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Good evening, Mr. Markovic. As I hope you recall, my name is Chris Gosnell, and I will be asking you some questions on behalf of Mr. Borovcanin. Would you please state your full name and date of birth for the record, please?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Jovo Markovic. I was born on the 30th of October, 1974.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, your report is now before the Chamber, so we won't be going through it chapter and verse. I would like to ask you a few questions to clarify and highlight some aspects of the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have Exhibit 4D617 on e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, this is your curriculum vitae, and I would just like to ask you a few questions about your curriculum vitae. Could you tell us what period of time you attended the military academy in Belgrade?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was at the academy from 1993 until 1997, which is when I graduated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Did you develop any specialisation while you were studying at the military academy?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. In the course of my education at the military academy, I was educated in the centre for communications or information and electronic surveillance. The course programme had to do with that of an electro technician.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, I know you speak English quite well, and so you understand my question immediately and can respond right away. I would simply ask you to observe a slight pause after the end of my question so that the translators can finish translating. Thank you. Did you have occasion during those studies to work with portable radio devices?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the things that we studied at the military academy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And what did you do after graduating from the military academy?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: After graduating, I joined the Republika Srpska army in 1997. I was on active duty then.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how long did you remain with the Republika Srpska army?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As a member of the Republika Srpska army, well, I remained there until 2007, which is when I moved from the army of Republika Srpska to the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could you simply repeat the last part of your answer? Moved from the army of Republika Srpska to what institution?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: As is well known, in 2'05, 2'06, there is a transition. The law in Bosnia and Herzegovina was changed, and the army of Republika Srpska became an integral part of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which were established in the 16th January, 2006. And all members of the Republika Srpska army at that time automatically became members of the armed forces of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Can we look at page 2 of this document, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, we see here that you rose up through the ranks of the VRS. Could you describe the various promotions and positions you held in the VRS?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. After I was received into the active duty service of the Republika Srpska army, I was made commander of the signalling company in the 108th Infantry Brigade. I spent about two years in that position. I was made the chief of communications in that same brigade. In the meantime, I finished cryptographic school at the military academy. It was in the school centre for communications, information, technology, and electronics surveillance. I held that post for two years, after which I became commander of an independent communications platoon. It was directly subordinated to the General Staff of the army of Republika Srpska. While performing my duties as a commander of the communications company, the company I was in command of was responsible for establishing communications, of maintaining communications, for the needs of the army of Republika Srpska. The communications systems used were stationary. I should emphasize this fact. They weren't mobile. And also within my unit, there was cryptographic station working for the needs of the Republika Srpska army General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Sir, let me ask you. You say that you use stationary communications devices. Did you have occasion also to use portable communications devices, or did you use only stationary communication devices?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: My unit used stationary devices, centrals and relay devices; but when performing their regular daily activities we used mobile radio units that used frequencies of 140 to 180 megahertz, wavelengths of up to 2 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And what position did you assume after being the commander of the communications platoon that you've just described?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: After working as the company commander, I started working in the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. I worked there in the verifications centre of the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska. This centre controlled weapons. When I say "controlled weapons," I am referring to the military part of the Dayton Agreement, Article 2 and 4. Article 2 has to do with establishing trust within the B&H; it's similar to the Birac document from 1994 and 1999; and Article 4 had to do with controlling weapons exclusively, weapons referred to in the Dayton Agreement. It's very similar to the agreement on conventional forces in Europe.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, in that capacity, did you have any experience or use portable communication devices?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, we also used mobile radio units there of minor capacity, since the need wasn't that great. But when controlling weapons, we used mobile radios so that the members of this mission could communicate with each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in the course of those responsibilities, did you have occasion to come in contact with the radio communication devices that had been in use over the previous, let's say, 20 years?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, your -- well, perhaps you could elaborate and tell us what kind of contact you had or what you learned about those radio communications devices?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll go back a bit when I was the commander of the platoon and the chief of communications in the 108th Infantry Brigade. In 1997 and 1998, we worked on decommissioning weapons, old weapons, damaged weapons, and radio devices, weapons, too, but radio devices. I was responsible exclusively for radio devices that were used in the war and that were no longer of use -- or could no longer be used. There were huge quantities of radio devices that were no longer used because they couldn't be used or they were defective. We received radio devices from all sides, from officers, soldiers who are either still members of the Republika Srpska army or were former members of that army. They would bring in such radio devices in order to get rid of them in a certain sense; and on such occasions, I had contact with various kinds of devices, radio devices that had the same frequencies or they used the same frequencies. They were wavelengths of 2 metres, of 0.7 metres that these devices used. And when I came in to see such devices, I noticed that the faults consisted of poor batteries that could practically not be used. Often, mistakes were made when using such devices. The antennas had been exchanged, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Sorry for interjecting. Will you kindly just slow down a little bit for the interpreters and for the record.

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I'll repeat some of what I said. I came to see various radio devices. I also came to see devices that used wavelengths of 2 metres and devices that used wavelengths of 0.7 metres. As I have already said, such devices often had batteries that were very weak or that couldn't be used anymore, rechargeable batteries, for example.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I see from your CV that you were also a member of a United Nations mission. Can you tell us when that was?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I was a member of the peace mission of the UN in Ethiopia and Eritrea as a military observer in 2005 and 2006.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And did you have occasion while working for that mission to use portable communication devices?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. This was part of my daily work over there because when performing tasks of any kind in the field, it was necessary to have a mobile radio unit. This was necessary for each member. If one was using a vehicle, it was necessary to have at least one portable radio device.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now, before this report that you've prepared for us and for the Chamber, had you previously prepared audibility reports concerning portable communication devices, and if so, in what context?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. It was also part of my education at the military academy. Naturally, after the military academy, after I had graduated when serving in the RS army, whenever one was to establish communications -- well, first, you would check to see that it was possible to establish communications by using a radio device. One would use a map for such purposes. It all depended on the configuration on the ground. When we confirmed that it was possible to establish communications by referring to the map, in such cases we would then actually check to see whether this was possible by going into the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you for that information. Now, how was it that you came to write this report? Were you contacted by the Defence?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The Ministry of the Interior was contacted by the Defence team; and afterwards, on behalf of the Ministry of Defence [as interpreted] I drafted this report that you have here today.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, I understand that the transcript says -- you first referred to the Ministry of the Interior, but then there is a reference to the Ministry of Defence. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No. I said that the Ministry of the Interior was contacted by the Defence team. Mr. Sasa was the specific person, and then I started drafting the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Let's now move to your report itself. What radio devices did you test for this report?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: I used two types of devices in both cases, Motorola devices. The first device uses a 2-metre wavelength, and the second one a wavelength of 0.7 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And what led you to test these two devices?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, two things. Firstly, on the basis of the photograph that I saw, I recognized that it was a portable radio device on the base of the antenna on the device. It was a radio device that used a wavelength of 0.7 metres. Because those antennas are quite specific, it's difficult to mistake those antennas for other types of antennas. And the second thing is that I also used a device, a radio device, that used a wavelength of 2 metres because these are the wavelengths that were used in the former Yugoslavia, in all parts of the former Yugoslavia, and that includes Bosnia and Herzegovina, naturally.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And to your knowledge, were there any other handheld radio devices that were in use in the former Yugoslavia in 1995 other than the two that you've just identified?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No, not as far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, is audibility between two radio devices determined by the specifications of the transmitter or the receiver?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On the whole, by the transmitter because the receiver has standard characteristics.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. So how does identifying the receiving device - assuming that that's the case - how does that assist you in understanding the nature of the transmitting device?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, for the receiver to receive a signal from a transmitting device, the characteristics should be identical. If they're not and if they don't use the same wavelengths, then reception is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, can you tell us what the -- well, you've used the word "wavelengths" or it's been translated as "wavelengths." Can you tell us what the frequency of the two devices -- the frequency range of the two devices that you tested is?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The frequency for the wavelength of 2 metres - and this naturally depends on the producer - is between 140 and 180 megahertz. So that is the range of frequencies. When it comes to wavelengths of 0.7 metres - and again, this all depends on the make of the device in question - the frequency is between 400 and 460 megahertz.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you conduct a field test using these two devices?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have 4D607 on e-court, please. Page 15 of the -- of both versions. Can we zoom in just a little bit more, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, this concerns according to the title the radio device operating at the 0.7-metres wavelength. That is the Motorola OP 30. I wonder if you can just tell us your conclusion. Now, based on your field testing, can you please tell us the audibility result as between point 6, which you've identified as a place called Hrncici, and point 1, which is identified as Sandici meadow?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The test that was carried out in the field between point 1 - which is at Sandici meadow; the geographic coordinates were given in the report - and point 6, the village of Hrncici, which is 4.000 metres from point 1 -- well, when we carried out this test, we checked the communication system by setting up a radio device with my colleague at point 1, and I drove towards point number 6 in this particular case, and we checked the communications system every 20 to 30 seconds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where is point 6, Mr. Gosnell or Mr. Markovic? Can you follow the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Perhaps we could zoom in a little more tightly on the document, and then it should become clear. I think we can go even tighter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: So, sir, perhaps you could explain. What is the significance -- or perhaps I said be more accurate and ask you, how is it that you determined point 6? What is the significance of point 6 on annex 9?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Point 6 is a geographic location, and at this point all communications in the vehicle -- in a vehicle come to an end. I stopped at point 6 and tried to establish the same communications outside of the vehicle, and that is where I determined that it was possible to establish communication. The value was 2 through 1 for that kind of communication. And this is a standard assessment. 2 through 1, 2/1, means that audibility on a scale of 1 to 5 was 2, but it was practically incomprehensible. On a scale of 1 to 5, comprehension was level 1. Practically incomprehensible. I'd just like to emphasize that in the vehicle itself it was impossible to establish communications.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And staying with this annex 9, could you please tell us what this audibility result was between that same spot, point 6, and point 2, which is the Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Between point 2 and point 6, it was impossible to establish communications, both in and out of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could you hear anything at all based on a test between those two points?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And how did you actually do that test?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: The test was performed in the same way as the test between points 1 and 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And in respect of these two results or these two references points, between point 6 and point 1 and point 6 and point 2, did you reach the same result in respect of the other device as well?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The testing was performed with both radio sets, and the results that I obtained were absolutely the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Looking at this map, we see something that looks like pixels on the map. Could you explain what that represents?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Looking at the map, the areas depicted by colour red are the areas where it is absolutely possible to establish communication. The areas in blue are the areas where it is only theoretically possible to establish communication. However, the communication is poor or extremely poor. Grey areas are areas where it is absolutely impossible to establish any sort of communication with the devices that I had at my disposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, how did you generate this pixilated representation on the map?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: We received this map, or actually, we generated this map by using a programme called HerTZ Mapper that we normally use in the Ministry of the Interior in the crime prevention police administration, and this programme is used to establish the connectivity of radio communications. The data were obtained in the following way: We entered initial data in the already-existing digital maps, and the data that we used were as follows: Geographic coordinates from the points already represented, and these we obtained using the Garmin GPS device.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Well, perhaps I could just cut to the key question, which is, does this programme incorporate or include topographical data?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: This programme does not provide the exact topographical data. It only represents the most characteristics points, which means that it doesn't correspond totally to topographic maps, which provide a lot more details.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. And how would you compare the accuracy of the pixilated representation of audibility and a field test testing audibility?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: In this case, as depicted on this map, between points 1 and 6, the results coincide within the vehicle, which means that there is no connectivity, whereas outside of the vehicle some sort of communication could be established, but the comprehensibility of that communication was low or none. And between points 2 and 6, as shown on the map, there was no connectivity either in or outside of the vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And leaving aside for the moment this particular map, could you tell us in general terms whether there were any drawbacks related to the HerTZ Mapper audibility test and a field audibility test?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could all the microphones not be in use please be switched off. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, of course. The difference between these two tests depends on some other factors; i.e., there are some other factors that have an impact on the physical verification of communication. What we see on the map are the ideal conditions, which means that the radio device works at its maximum strength of 5 watts under the ideal weather conditions and that it is outside of the vehicle. Whilst -- when we were checking communications on -- in the field, the influence of all the aforementioned factors was present: Weather conditions; the strength of the device, i.e., the frequency that it was working on; the battery, whether it was fully charged or just half-charged; the shelf life of the battery - this is what I mean when I say the battery; and also, one of major influencing factors is whether an attempt to establish communication is made in the vehicle or outside of it. All these factors have an impact on the attempt to establish communication. And to be even more precise on that, when we used the programme, we used the ideal conditions, both weather conditions and the condition of the device. While we were testing communication in the field, all the negative factors were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Could we please have annex 7 on e-court, please. It's two pages previous before annex 9, and please zoom in tightly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, sir, are the points 1, 2, and 6 the same coordinates as appeared on the previous map?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And does this map in any way illustrate what you've just described about the relationship between the two types of testing?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And, sir, what were the weather conditions like when you conducted your field test on the 17th of September, 2008?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: On that day, it was partly cloudy.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And on a scale of 1 to 10, how would you rate the atmospheric conditions in terms of relative to the ideal conditions for transmission?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: According to my free estimate, I would say somewhere between 8 and 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Can we go to page 2 of the report, please, in both English and B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Now, at the bottom of the page, you say: "It has also been established that at the time in the said area there were no active amplifying inter-stations that could amplify the range of the radio connection. Rather, the radio connection was used exclusively in simplex mode." Can you please share with us how you know that or how you reached that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Before embarking on the connection testing in the locations that were given, we had visited the police station in Bratunac. The two of us were received by the deputy commander of the police station, and we put the same question to him, namely, whether there were any amplifying inter-stations and whether there were any at the moment when we were asking on the 17th of September, 2008. In other words, whether there had been before and whether there were at that moment. He called a member of the police staff who was a signals man at the time. He told us that in the territory covered by the Bratunac police station and in the territory of Bratunac municipality there had never existed any amplifying inter-stations. There were done during the existence of the former Yugoslavia, none during the conflict, and there were none at the time when we spoke to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Sir, do you know Mr. Borovcanin?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Have you ever met him?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: And do you have any reason to be biased in his favour because of his former association with the Ministry of the Interior?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Has anyone pressured you in relation to the results that are expressed in your report?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: All right. Sir, I just have one last question for you, and it relates to page 1 of your report. Is there a correction that you wish to make in relation to point 2?

utterances.speaker: JOVO MARKOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. There are corrections on the pages 1 and 3 that concern the geographic coordinates on point 2. The first coordinate, it says here "92, 8 seconds," and this is a typo. It should be "42, 8 seconds." On page 3, I would like to make the same correction. Under item, 3, it should again read "42, 8 seconds."

utterances.speaker: MR. GOSNELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: No question for the witness, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Nikolic? Or Mr. Bourgon, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I would ask with the leave of the Court to begin the cross-examination tomorrow morning. The reason being is I have a technical problem with a map that I prepared. I have an extract, and looking at it now, it doesn't look very good, and I need to seek the assistance of the registrar. I could be ready in the morning first thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Mr. Bourgon. We appreciate you have a problem. We will start with your cross-examination tomorrow. Thank you. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 31st day of October, 2008, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 6.50 p.m.,
